title: Satellites: Eyes in the Sky
summary: Learn how Sputnik's historic 1957 launch sparked the Space Race and led to the thousands of satellites that quietly support modern life today.
poll: Would you rather help design a satellite or ride inside a rocket into space?

versions.title: Satellites: Eyes in the Sky
versions.text:
High above Earth, a small machine flies. It goes around and around our world. Big rockets sent it up there.

It can do many jobs. One helps phones work. One takes pictures of clouds. One helps maps work on your phone.

Long ago, there were none at all up there. Then in 1957, one land sent up the very first one, called Sputnik. It was small and round. It could only send out a beep.

This first one showed that the plan could work. Soon more lands sent up their own.

Today, many of these fly high above us. They help us talk. They help us watch the news. They help us find our way. They help us each day, even when we do not see them.

Long ago, there were none at all up in space. Then in 1957, one country sent up the very first one. It was small, round, and made of shiny metal. It could only send out a simple beeping sound as it flew.

A machine like this can do many jobs for people on Earth. One helps our phones work, no matter where we are. One takes pictures of clouds and storms from high above. One helps maps work on our phones and shows us which way to go.

Long ago, none of these were orbiting in space at all. Then in 1957, one country sent up the very first one, called Sputnik. It was small, round, and made of shiny metal. It could only send out a simple beeping sound as it flew overhead.

That first one showed people around the world that this new plan could truly work. Soon, other countries began building and sending up their own machines as well.

Today, thousands of these circle high above us in space. They help us talk, watch the news, and find our way around unfamiliar places. They quietly help us every single day, even when we cannot see them at all.

versions.text:
A satellite is a machine that flies above Earth and circles our planet again and again. It moves much like the moon does. Engineers launch each one into space using huge, powerful rockets.

A satellite can do many jobs for people on Earth. One helps our phones and TVs work, no matter where we are. One takes pictures of clouds and storms from high up. One helps maps work on our phones and guides us to where we want to go.

Long ago, none of these existed anywhere in space. Then in 1957, the Soviet Union sent up the very first one, called Sputnik. It was small, round, and made of polished metal. It could only send out a simple beeping signal as it flew overhead.

That first one proved to people around the world that this new plan could truly succeed. Soon, other countries began building and sending up their own, eager to explore this new frontier.

Today, thousands of these circle high above us in orbit. They help us talk, watch the news, and find our way in unfamiliar places. They quietly support our daily lives, even when we never actually see them flying by.

That first one proved to people around the entire world that this new plan could truly succeed. Soon, other countries began designing and sending up their own, eager to explore this exciting new frontier.

Today, thousands of satellites circle high above us in orbit around Earth. They help us talk, watch the news, and find our way in unfamiliar places with ease. They quietly support our daily lives, even though we never actually see them pass quietly overhead.

That first one proved to people around the entire world that this new plan could truly succeed. Soon, other countries began designing and sending up their own, eager to explore this exciting new frontier of space.

Another captures detailed pictures of clouds and storms from high above, helping forecasters predict the weather accurately. Another helps maps work correctly on our phones and guides travelers toward their intended place, wherever that happens to actually be.

Long ago, none of these existed anywhere in space. Then in 1957, the Soviet Union sent up the very first one, called Sputnik, into orbit around Earth. It was small, round, and made of polished metal. It could only send out a simple beeping signal as it circled overhead, yet this was a remarkable scientific achievement at the time.

That first one proved to people around the entire world that this new plan could truly succeed. Soon, other countries began designing and sending up their own satellites, eager to explore this exciting new frontier of space and achieve similar scientific breakthroughs.

versions.title: Satellites: Eyes in the Sky
versions.text:
A satellite is any object that orbits a larger body in space, held in place by gravity. The word usually refers to artificial machines humans launch above Earth. On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, into orbit. This single launch sparked what later became known across the world as the Space Race between the Soviet Union and the United States.

Sputnik itself was remarkably simple. It was a polished metal sphere about the size of a beach ball. It transmitted only a steady radio beep as it circled the planet. Despite its simplicity, Sputnik's success stunned scientists and governments worldwide. It proved that humans could place objects in stable orbit around Earth, something many had long dreamed about but never actually achieved.

In the decades since that historic launch, satellite technology has advanced enormously. Communications satellites now relay phone calls, television broadcasts, and internet signals across vast distances almost instantly. This connects people who live on opposite sides of the world. Weather satellites capture continuous images of clouds and storms. This gives forecasters far more warning before dangerous weather arrives, helping save lives in many communities. Navigation satellites, part of systems like GPS, let phones and cars calculate precise locations almost anywhere on Earth, guiding travelers to places they have never visited before.

Today, thousands of satellites orbit our planet, supporting communication, weather forecasting, navigation, and scientific research. Few people realize how often they depend on this invisible network circling silently overhead. Yet modern life would look dramatically different without it. Scientists also use satellites to study distant planets, track changes in Earth's climate, and monitor forests and oceans from high above, gathering information that would be nearly impossible to collect from the ground alone using only older, more traditional scientific methods alone back then.

keyWords.definition: the curved path an object follows as it circles a larger body in space
keyWords.example: The spacecraft entered a stable orbit around Mars after its long journey.

keyWords.definition: a competition between rivals to achieve something first
keyWords.example: The two scientists were in a friendly race to finish their experiment first.

questions.stem: What is the central idea of this passage?
options: Sputnik's 1957 launch began the Space Race and led to the vast satellite network humans depend on today
the Space Race ended before Sputnik was ever launched
satellites today perform only a single simple task
the United States launched Sputnik before the Soviet Union did
questions.why: The passage traces how Sputnik's 1957 launch sparked the Space Race and ultimately led to today's widespread satellite network.

wrong.B: The passage shows the Space Race began after Sputnik's launch.
wrong.C: The passage describes satellites performing many varied tasks.
wrong.D: The passage credits the Soviet Union, not the United States, with Sputnik.

questions.stem: According to the passage, on what date did the Soviet Union launch Sputnik 1?
options: October 4th of the year 1957
July 20th of the year 1969
April 12th of the year 1961
September 1st of the year 1945
questions.why: The passage specifically states that Sputnik 1 was launched on October 4, 1957.

wrong.B: The passage does not give that later date for Sputnik's launch.
wrong.C: The passage does not give that date for Sputnik's launch.
wrong.D: The passage does not give that earlier date for Sputnik's launch.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, how long did it take Sputnik to orbit Earth once?
options: about twenty-four hours
about one full week
about ninety-eight seconds
about ninety-eight minutes
questions.why: The passage states that Sputnik circled the planet every ninety-eight minutes.

wrong.A: The passage does not give a twenty-four hour orbit time.
wrong.B: The passage does not give a one-week orbit time.
wrong.C: The passage says minutes, not seconds, for this orbit time.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why Sputnik's launch is described as sparking a 'Space Race'?
options: it caused every other country in the world to immediately stop all rocket research
it created intense competition between two rival nations eager to achieve dominance in space exploration
it proved that only one single nation would ever build satellites
it ended all further cooperation between scientists around the globe
questions.why: The passage shows Sputnik's success sparked fierce rivalry between the Soviet Union and the United States in space exploration.

wrong.A: The passage shows other countries soon launched their own satellites.
wrong.C: The passage shows multiple nations eventually built satellites.
wrong.D: The passage focuses on rivalry, not scientific cooperation, between two nations.

questions.stem: What is most likely the reason the passage describes satellites as an 'invisible network' that most people rarely notice?
options: because satellites quietly support daily tasks like calls and navigation without most people ever seeing them
because satellites are actually too small for scientists to detect accurately
because satellites stopped working properly many years ago
because very few satellites currently orbit the Earth today
questions.why: The passage suggests satellites work constantly and quietly in the background, which is why people rarely think about them.

wrong.B: The passage never claims satellites are undetectable by scientists.
wrong.C: The passage shows satellites continue working reliably today.
wrong.D: The passage states thousands of satellites currently orbit Earth.

questions.stem: What does the word 'conclusively' mean as it is used in this passage?
options: in a way that leaves no doubt or question
in a way that happens very slowly over time
in a way that is easily reversed or undone
in a manner that affects only a small area
questions.why: In the passage, conclusively describes how clearly and certainly Sputnik proved that satellites could orbit Earth.

wrong.B: Conclusively does not describe a slow process in this passage.
wrong.C: Conclusively does not mean easily reversed in this passage.
wrong.D: Conclusively does not refer to the size of an affected area.

questions.stem: How does the passage's structure help explain satellites' importance today?
options: it moves from Sputnik's historic 1957 launch, through decades of advancement, to today's reliance on satellites for countless tasks
it presents two opposing arguments about whether satellites should exist
it offers a step-by-step guide for building a satellite at home
it ranks several countries by how many satellites they currently own
questions.why: The passage builds historical context from Sputnik's launch through today's extensive satellite use, showing growing importance over time.

wrong.B: The passage presents one historical account, not opposing arguments.
wrong.C: The passage does not provide satellite-building instructions.
wrong.D: The passage never ranks countries by satellite ownership.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is a likely long-term effect of advancing satellite technology?
options: people will keep depending on satellites for many important daily tasks
fewer countries will likely choose to launch new satellites in the future
satellites will eventually and completely stop orbiting Earth altogether
scientists will probably stop using satellites for weather forecasting entirely
questions.why: The passage suggests satellite technology will keep advancing, deepening our reliance on it for many important tasks.

wrong.B: The passage shows satellite technology continuing to advance, not decline.
wrong.C: The passage never suggests satellites will stop orbiting.
wrong.D: The passage shows weather satellites remain in active use.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how Sputnik's launch sparked the Space Race, and describe how satellite technology has advanced since 1957. Use details from the passage.
checklist: Explains that the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957, sparking the Space Race with the United States
Explains that gravity held Sputnik in a stable orbit, proving humans could successfully place objects in space
Describes how satellite technology has advanced to support communication, weather forecasting, navigation, and scientific research today
HIGH.modelAnswer: On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, into orbit around Earth, sparking the Space Race between the Soviet Union and the United States. Sputnik was a simple, polished metal sphere held in a stable orbit by gravity, transmitting only a steady radio beep, yet its success proved conclusively that humans could place objects in orbit. In the decades since, satellite technology has advanced enormously. Communications satellites relay calls and internet signals, weather satellites warn forecasters of dangerous storms, and navigation satellites, part of systems like GPS, guide travelers almost anywhere on Earth. Today, thousands of satellites support communication, weather forecasting, navigation, and scientific research, even though most people rarely notice this invisible network circling silently overhead.

LOW.stem: What would most likely happen if no lands had ever sent up a machine like this?
options: maps, calls, and weather pictures might not work the way they do today
the moon would stop moving around Earth
rockets would never have been built at all
people would stop talking to each other completely
LOW.why: Since these machines help maps, calls, and weather pictures work, not having any would likely change how those things work today.

wrong.B: The passage never connects this machine to the moon's own movement.
wrong.C: The passage shows rockets were already used for other things too.
wrong.D: The passage never suggests people would stop talking entirely.

LOW.stem: Why did the passage mention that the very first machine could only send out a simple beep?
options: to prove that beeps are the loudest sound a machine can make
to argue that the first machine was a complete failure
to explain why rockets are expensive to build
to show how simple the first one was compared to what these machines do today
LOW.why: This detail highlights how far this technology has come, from a simple beep to helping with calls, maps, and more.

wrong.A: The passage never compares beeps to other loud sounds.
wrong.B: The passage shows the first one was a success, not a failure.
wrong.C: The passage never discusses the cost of rockets.

LOW.stem: How is the first machine from 1957 similar to the many machines flying above us today?
options: b
both circle around and around Earth, high above us
o
t
LOW.why: The passage shows both the first machine and today's machines share the basic job of circling Earth, even though today's machines do far more.

wrong.A: The passage says photos came later, not with the first machine.
wrong.C: The passage says rockets, not balloons, launched these machines.
wrong.D: The passage says other lands later built their own too.

LOW.stem: What is the best reason the passage says these machines 'help us every single day'?
options: because so many of them now circle Earth, doing jobs like helping maps and calls work
because they are given away for free to every family
because they can only be used once a year
because each machine does only one single job forever
LOW.why: The passage explains thousands of these machines circle Earth, constantly supporting things like calls, news, and maps.

wrong.B: The passage never says these are given away for free.
wrong.C: The passage shows these help every single day, not once a year.
wrong.D: The passage shows a single machine can do several different jobs.

MID.stem: What would most likely happen to weather forecasting without satellites?
options: storms would completely stop forming entirely without satellites in orbit
forecasters would instantly predict the exact weather with perfect accuracy
satellites would urgently need to be replaced by airplanes immediately
forecasters would likely have far less warning before dangerous storms arrive
MID.why: Since weather satellites give forecasters advance warning of storms, losing them would likely reduce that warning time significantly.

wrong.A: The passage never suggests satellites cause or prevent storms.
wrong.B: The passage shows satellites currently provide helpful, not perfect, warning.
wrong.C: The passage never suggests replacing satellites with airplanes.

MID.stem: Why might the passage emphasize that Sputnik's success 'stunned' scientists and governments worldwide?
options: to show how surprising and significant this achievement truly was at the time
to suggest that scientists had always expected this exact outcome
to argue that Sputnik's launch caused widespread panic and fear
to prove that satellites had already existed many years earlier
MID.why: The word 'stunned' highlights that few people expected this success, making it a landmark achievement in history.

wrong.B: The passage shows this success was unexpected, not anticipated.
wrong.C: The passage never mentions panic or fear resulting from the launch.
wrong.D: The passage places Sputnik as the very first satellite.

MID.stem: How are communications satellites and weather satellites similar, based on the passage?
options: both were launched in the exact same year as Sputnik itself
both can only function during the daytime hours of the day
both orbit Earth and perform a specific, useful job for people below
both were designed exclusively for use in just one single country
MID.why: The passage shows both types of satellites share the basic role of orbiting Earth while serving a specific, helpful purpose.

wrong.A: The passage never ties both types to Sputnik's exact launch year.
wrong.B: The passage never limits satellite function to daytime only.
wrong.D: The passage describes satellites serving people broadly, not one country.

MID.stem: What is most likely the reason the passage describes several different kinds of satellites, such as weather and navigation satellites?
options: to show the wide variety of important jobs satellites perform for people
to prove that each kind of satellite requires its own separate rocket launch pad
to suggest that most satellites are rarely useful in daily life
to argue that only one kind of satellite should exist at all
MID.why: Describing several kinds of satellites helps show just how many different important tasks this technology now performs.

wrong.B: The passage never discusses separate launch pads for each kind.
wrong.C: The passage presents satellites as very useful in daily life.
wrong.D: The passage never argues for limiting satellites to one kind.

HIGH.stem: What would most likely have happened if Sputnik's launch had failed in 1957?
options: satellites would have likely been invented decades earlier instead
the Space Race and the overall pace of satellite development might have unfolded quite differently afterward
gravity itself would have stopped working as a scientific force
the Soviet Union would have immediately given up all rocket research entirely
HIGH.why: Since Sputnik's success sparked the Space Race, a failed launch might have changed how and when satellite technology developed.

wrong.A: The passage places Sputnik as the earliest satellite, not a later one.
wrong.C: The passage never suggests gravity itself was affected.
wrong.D: The passage shows satellite research continuing to grow after 1957.

HIGH.stem: Why might the passage specifically note that many experts had 'seriously doubted' stable orbit was possible before Sputnik?
options: to suggest that Sputnik's launch was secretly faked by the Soviet Union all along
to argue that most experts were always fully confident orbit was achievable
to emphasize just how remarkable and unexpected Sputnik's successful launch truly was
to prove that not a single scientist ever studied orbit before 1957
HIGH.why: This detail highlights how groundbreaking Sputnik's success felt, given that many experts had doubted it was even possible.

wrong.A: The passage presents Sputnik's launch as a real, verified achievement.
wrong.B: The passage says experts doubted it, not felt confident.
wrong.D: The passage implies scientists had studied orbit and doubted its success.

HIGH.stem: How does Sputnik compare with today's satellites, based on the passage?
options: both were launched by the exact same country on the exact same calendar date
both can only ever send out a simple beeping signal
both were designed specifically only to study distant planets
both orbit Earth, but today's satellites perform far more advanced and varied tasks
HIGH.why: The passage shows both share the basic concept of orbiting Earth, though today's satellites handle vastly more advanced tasks than Sputnik's simple beep.

wrong.A: The passage shows many countries now launch satellites of their own.
wrong.B: The passage shows today's satellites send far more complex signals.
wrong.C: The passage shows satellites perform many varied tasks beyond planet study.

HIGH.stem: What is most likely the author's purpose in writing this passage?
options: to explain how Sputnik's launch led to today's satellite technology
to firmly convince readers that the Soviet Union was a better country than the United States
to strongly argue that satellite technology has caused far more harm than good
to simply entertain readers with an invented story about outer space
HIGH.why: The passage traces satellite history from Sputnik to today, aiming to inform readers about its lasting importance.

wrong.B: The passage never ranks one nation as better than the other.
wrong.C: The passage presents satellites as broadly beneficial, not harmful.
wrong.D: The passage presents real historical facts, not an invented story.
